series: Launching a Cosmetics Brand in Korea
approvedBy: Preview draft from user-provided source — not yet approved for publication

cards.headline: The Factory Made It. Who Files the Report?
body: For a cosmetics OEM, production and sales numbers can tell different stories.
cards.promise: See the duties that stay with you
cards.takeaway: The responsible distributor must track what the OEM actually produced.
cards.design: A premium navy cover with a large cream jar and three stylized source records; one gold line connects factory to brand, with no fake verification badge.

cards.headline: Which Number Is the Production Figure?

body.text: The purchase order, not finished output.
Finished units the OEM actually completed.
Units sold online, not production volume.

cards.takeaway: Report the 900 units actually produced, not the 1,000 ordered or 400 sold.
cards.design: Three scaled horizontal bars using actual counts; highlight the 900-produced bar with gold and a plain-language answer.

cards.headline: Production Year Beats Delivery Date
body: The OEM makes the cream in December 2026.
The brand receives it in January 2027.
Treat it as 2026 production, not 2027 receipts.
Report 2026 production by the end of February 2027.
cards.takeaway: Check production dates and use the name in the product standard document.
cards.design: A prominent December-to-January timeline, with the production-year tag anchoring the December date and the statutory reporting deadline below.

cards.headline: Zero Sales Does Not Mean Zero Production

body.text: Where the domestic OEM completed the goods, the responsible distributor reports actual production even if sales are zero.
A distributor registered to sell domestically manufactured cosmetics reports “no production” when no domestic goods were made.

cards.takeaway: A company registered only for imported cosmetics is outside this domestic reporting route.
cards.design: Two contrasting full-height columns, product boxes for manufactured goods versus a blank production ledger, with the importer-only condition separate beneath.

cards.headline: Training Follows the Registered Manager

body.text: The responsible manager generally completes the first course within six months of beginning the work.
After initial training, the manager must complete refresher training once each year.
The company representative cannot complete the named manager’s mandatory training for them.

cards.takeaway: Check actual completion certificates for the person named on the registration.
cards.design: A large completion-certificate graphic flanked by a six-month clock and an annual calendar; registration name is the focal point.

cards.headline: Registration Is Not the Finish Line.
body: Production reports, manager training and safety follow different clocks.
cards.takeaway: A calendar should be built from source records, not just the registration date.
cards.design: Quiet oversized serif-free typography with one horizontal fine gold rule and generous negative space; no boxes.

cards.headline: A Skin-Reaction Message Starts a Record

body.text: Note onset and batch ID if known.
Pass the facts to the named manager.

cards.takeaway: Keep the report even before a medical cause has been established.
cards.design: Flowing four-node chain, from a customer message to a responsible manager, with no invented medical conclusion.

cards.headline: Safety Information Has Two Reporting Clocks
head: Report
Due

body.text: Jan–Jun information: by July 31 of the same year.
Jul–Dec information: by January 31 of the next year.
E.g., serious cases: within 15 days of awareness.

cards.takeaway: The rapid clock begins when the company learns a qualifying reportable fact.
cards.design: Large 15 DAYS accent plus a simple three-row ruled calendar table; note that specified foreign government actions may also trigger rapid reporting.

cards.headline: No Safety Information? The Exception Is Narrow

body.text: File the semiannual regular report even if there is no safety information; submit “nothing to report” electronically.
With two or fewer regular workers, a distributor that sells only cosmetic soap it manufactures itself may omit the regular report.

cards.takeaway: An OEM-made moisturizing cream does not meet the soap-only exception.
cards.design: Visually separate a broad mandatory branch and a tightly scoped exception with both AND conditions conspicuously readable.

cards.headline: Which Records Should You Compare First?

body.text: Share any available registration certificate, OEM production-completion details, past filing receipt or new manager eligibility records.
The preliminary check looks at production year, registered manager and missing records. Drafting or filing is separately agreed.

cards.takeaway: Ask Ethos Administrative Attorney Office for a free preliminary document check.
cards.design: Two unequal panels: documents stacked to the left, magnifier over mismatched dates to the right; a restrained bottom one-sentence CTA.
